en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
The Chapter on False Speech, 3.
The Training Rule on Slander.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the group of six monks were engaging in slander against monks who had fallen into quarreling, brawling, and disputes.

Having heard something from one person, they would report it to another for the purpose of creating a rift; having heard something from another, they would report it to the first for the purpose of creating a rift.
Because of this, quarrels that had not yet arisen arose, and quarrels that had already arisen led to further increase and expansion.
Those bhikkhus who were of few desires... [and so on]... complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:

"How can the group-of-six bhikkhus, when bhikkhus have fallen into quarreling, brawling, and disputes, engage in slander? Having heard something from one, they report it to the other for the purpose of dividing him;
having heard something from the other, they report it to the first for the purpose of dividing him."
“Because of that, quarrels that have not yet arisen arise, and quarrels that have already arisen lead to further increase and expansion.
Then those monks, having rebuked the group-of-six monks in many ways, reported this matter to the Blessed One. … [The Buddha said:
“Is it true, monks, that you [acted] thus when the monks were engaged in quarreling, brawling, and falling into disputes?”
"Do you practice slander—having heard something from this person, do you report it to that person to create a rift between them;
or having heard something from that person, do you report it to this person to create a rift between them?
For by such means, quarrels that have not yet arisen arise, and quarrels that have already arisen lead to further increase and expansion?"

“It is true, Blessed One. The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them: “… How can you, foolish men, engage in slander against monks who have fallen into quarreling, brawling, and disputes? This will not lead to the welfare of many people, nor to the happiness of many people; it will not lead to the benefit, welfare, and happiness of devas and humans. [The Buddha spoke in many ways in rebuke. Then he addressed the monks: “Monks, this is an offense of wrong-doing for a monk who, knowing that a dispute has arisen among other monks, engages in slander by saying: ‘This is what they say about you; go and find out. Or if he says: ‘I heard this from such-and-such a person; go and find out. Or if he says: ‘I suspect this of them; go and find out. Or if he says: ‘I do not know whether this is so or not; go and find out. Or if he says: ‘Go and find out whether this is so or not. Or if he says: ‘Go and find out whether this is true or false. Having heard this from one person, you will report it to another for the sake of creating division; having heard this from another, you will report it to the first for the sake of creating division.
By this means, quarrels that have not yet arisen arise, and quarrels that have already arisen lead to further increase and expansion.
This, foolish men, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence.
Or for the increase of those who are already confident...
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule thus:
"In malicious talebearing toward a monk, there is an offense of expiation."
Slander (*pesuñña*) occurs in two ways: either by one who desires to be dear or by one who intends to cause a schism.
One employs slander in ten ways: by birth, by name, by clan, by occupation, by craft, by illness, by gender, by defilement, by offense, and by abuse.
Birth is of two kinds: low birth and high birth.
Low birth is as follows:
The outcaste class, the bamboo-worker class, the hunter class, the chariot-maker class, and the scavenger class— this is called the low birth. The noble birth—
the warrior-noble class and the brahmin class— this is called the high birth.
…pe….
What is called “abuse” consists of two kinds of abuse: low abuse and high abuse.
An inferior insult is as follows:
"You are a camel! You are a ram! You are an ox! You are a donkey! You are an animal! You are destined for hell! There is no happy rebirth for you;
only an evil destiny is to be expected for you! Or [insults using] the syllable *ya* or the syllable *bha*, or with a basket-weaver's shuttle.
This is called an inferior insult.
A superior insult is as follows:

"You are wise, you are competent, you are intelligent, you are learned, you are an expounder of the Dhamma; there is no miserable destination for you; only a happy destination is to be expected for you. This is called a superior insult.

If one who is ordained, having heard it from another who is ordained, conveys malicious report to yet another who is ordained, saying, "So-and-so says of you: 'He is a caṇḍāla, a veṇa, a nesāda, a rathakāra, or a pukkusa,'" there is an offense for each word; for every word, it is a *pācittiya*.

If one who is ordained, having heard it from another who is ordained, conveys malicious report to yet another who is ordained, saying, "So-and-so says of you: 'He is a khattiya or a brāhmaṇa,'" there is an offense for each word; for every word, it is a *pācittiya*.
If one who is ordained, having heard it from another who is ordained, engages in malicious talebearing toward yet another who is ordained, saying:
"So-and-so says of you: 'He is a backbiter, a slanderer, a Dhaniṭṭhaka, a Saviṭṭhaka, a family-increaser,'" there is an offense for every statement;
for each statement, it is a *pācittiya*.

If one who is ordained, having heard it from another who is ordained, engages in malicious talebearing toward a third who is ordained, saying, "So-and-so says of you, 'He is protected by the Buddha, protected by the Dhamma, protected by the Saṅgha,'" there is an offense for every word; for each word, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

If one who is ordained, having heard it from another who is ordained, engages in malicious talebearing toward a third who is ordained, saying, "So-and-so says of you, 'He is a Kosiya, a Bhāradvāja,'" there is an offense for every word; for each word, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

If one who is ordained, having heard it from another who is ordained, conveys malicious talebearing to yet another who is ordained, saying, “So-and-so says of you: ‘He is a Gotama, a Moggallāna, a Kaccāna, or a Vāsiṭṭha,’” there is an offense for each word; for every word, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

If one who is ordained, having heard it from another who is ordained, conveys malicious talebearing to yet another who is ordained, saying, “So-and-so says of you: ‘He is a Koṭṭhaka, a refuse-disposer,’” there is an offense for each word; for every word, it is an offense of expiation.

If one who is ordained, having heard it from another who is ordained, engages in malicious talebearing toward yet another who is ordained, saying, "So-and-so says of you: 'He is a farmer, a merchant, or a cattle-herder,'" there is an offense for every word; for each word, there is an *pācittiya* offense.
If one who is ordained, having heard it from another who is ordained, engages in malicious talebearing toward yet another who is ordained, saying, "So-and-so says of you:
'He is a reed-worker, a potter, a weaver, a leather-worker, or a barber,'" there is an offense for every word.
Regarding the offense of expiation for speech:

if one who is fully ordained, having heard it from another who is fully ordained, engages in slander toward a third who is fully ordained, saying, "So-and-so says of you, 'He is a finger-counter, an accountant, a scribe,'" there is an offense for each word; that is, an offense of expiation for speech.
If one who is fully ordained, having heard it from another who is fully ordained, engages in slander toward a third who is fully ordained, saying, "So-and-so..."
“He says of him, ‘He is a leper, one with sores, one with scabs, one with consumption, one with chronic disease. There is an offense for each word; for each word, it is a *pācittiya*.

If one who is fully ordained, having heard it from another who is fully ordained, engages in malicious talebearing toward a third who is fully ordained, saying, “So-and-so says of you, ‘He is a diabetic,’” there is an offense for each word; for each word, it is a *pācittiya*.

If one who is ordained, having heard it from another who is ordained, engages in malicious talebearing toward yet another who is ordained, saying, "So-and-so says of you: 'He is too tall, too short, too dark, or too fair,'" there is an offense for every word; for each word, there is an *pācittiya*.

If one who is ordained, having heard it from another who is ordained, engages in malicious talebearing toward yet another who is ordained, saying, "So-and-so says of you: 'He is not too tall, not too short, not too dark, or not too fair,'" there is an offense for every word; for each word, there is an *pācittiya*.
If one who is ordained, having heard it from another who is ordained, engages in malicious talebearing toward yet another who is ordained,
saying, "So-and-so says of you that you are 'overcome by lust, overcome by hatred, overcome by delusion,'" there is an offense for every utterance;
for each utterance, it is a *pācittiya*.

If one who is ordained, having heard it from another who is ordained, engages in malicious talebearing toward yet another who is ordained, saying: "So-and-so says of you, 'He is free from lust, free from hatred, free from delusion,'" there is an offense for every word; for every word, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
If one who is ordained, having heard it from another who is ordained, engages in malicious talebearing toward yet another who is ordained, saying:

"So-and-so says of you, 'He has committed an offense entailing defeat (*pārājika*), he has committed an offense entailing suspension (*saṅghādisesa*), he has committed a serious offense (*thullaccaya*), he has committed an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*)..."
“He says: ‘He has committed an offense entailing confession (pāṭidesanīya), he has committed an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa), he has committed an offense of improper speech (dubbhāsita).
There is an offense for each word; for each word there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).

If one who is fully ordained, having heard it from another who is fully ordained, engages in slander against that fully ordained person, saying: “So-and-so says of you, ‘You are a stream-enterer,’” there is an offense for each word; for each word there is an offense entailing expiation.
If one who is fully ordained, having heard it from another who is fully ordained, engages in malicious talebearing toward yet another who is fully ordained, saying:

"So-and-so says of you: 'He is a camel, a ram, an ox, a donkey—a beast, a denizen of hell; there is no good destination for him, only a bad destination is to be expected for him,'" there is an offense for every utterance, an offense entailing expiation for each utterance.
If one who is ordained, having heard it from another who is ordained, engages in malicious talebearing toward yet another who is ordained, saying:
"So-and-so says of you: 'He is wise, competent, intelligent, learned, and an expounder of the Dhamma; there is no bad destination for him;
only a good destination is to be expected for him,'" there is an offense for every statement, a *pācittiya* for every statement.
Having heard it from one who is ordained, an ordained person engages in malicious talebearing toward another who is ordained, saying:
"So-and-so says, 'There are here some outcasts, bamboo-workers, hunters, chariot-makers, and scavengers'; he does not say anything else, he says that very thing.
For every word, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Having heard it from one who is fully ordained, a person who is fully ordained engages in malicious talebearing toward another who is fully ordained, saying:
"So-and-so says, 'There are here certain kṣatriyas and brahmins'; he does not say anything else, he says that very thing.
There is an offense for every word; for every word, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). …pe…
Having heard it from one who is ordained, an ordained person engages in malicious talebearing against another who is ordained, saying:
"So-and-so says, 'There are here certain wise, competent, intelligent, learned people who are preachers of the Dhamma; for them there is no bad destination;
only a good destination is to be expected for them. He does not say anything else; he says exactly that."
There is an offense of wrong-doing by speech for each instance of speech.
If one who is fully ordained, having heard it from another who is fully ordained, engages in malicious talebearing toward yet another who is fully ordained, saying:
"So-and-so says, 'Surely these are Caṇḍālas, Veṇas, Nesādas, Rathakāras, or Pukkusas'; he does not say anything else, he says that very thing."
“He says,” [if one says this], there is an offense of wrong-doing for each word.
If one who is fully ordained, having heard it from another who is fully ordained, engages in malicious talebearing toward a third who is fully ordained, saying:
“So-and-so says, ‘Surely those who are wise, competent, intelligent, learned, and preachers of the Dhamma’; he does not say anything else.”
"He says that very thing. There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for each word spoken.
If one who is fully ordained, having heard it from another who is fully ordained, engages in slander toward a third person who is fully ordained, saying:
"So-and-so says, 'We are not Caṇḍālas, Veṇas, Nesādas, Rathakāras, or Pukkusas'; he does not say anything else."
“He says that very thing. There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for each utterance.
If one who is fully ordained, having heard it from another who is fully ordained, engages in slander toward a third who is fully ordained, saying:

“So-and-so said, ‘We are not wise, competent, or intelligent, nor are we learned expounders of the Dhamma; there is no bad destination for us, only a good destination. [There is an offense of wrong-doing for each utterance.]
‘This is what we expect,’ he says; he does not say anything else, he says that very thing. There is an offense of wrong-doing for each word.

If one who is fully ordained, having heard it from another who is fully ordained, conveys malicious talebearing to one who is fully ordained, there is an offense entailing confession (pācittiya) for each word.
If one who is fully ordained, having heard it from another who is fully ordained, conveys malicious talebearing to one who is not fully ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one who is ordained, having heard it from one who is not ordained, conveys malicious talebearing to another who is ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one who is ordained, having heard it from one who is not ordained, conveys malicious talebearing to one who is not ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
There is no offense—
Nor for one who desires affection,
nor for one whose intention is to cause a schism,
nor for one who is insane.
"For one who is a first-offender":
the third training rule on malicious talebearing is concluded.
